I absolutely hate how much unaccountable power adults have over kids. I realize there are some pretty fundamental structural challenges that make this difficult, but I badly want the rules of the game to be rewritten so children can have true authorship over their lives.3

I want all the rules of every game to be rewritten so every being, no matter how small or weak, can be durably sheltered from the ravages of competition in its many forms: physical contests, status games, and yes, market competition. I want everyone to be free to blossom into whoever they would be without the pressure to fight to survive, with no one to make them afraid.

But the leftist instinct is often detrimental to its moral vision. The left finds power gross, and as many people have noted, it seems far more at home critiquing and deconstructing it than building and wielding it. Yet realizing the grand dream of the left, the rewriting of the rules, requires a staggeringly ambitious project to build and wield vast power.

If you’re one of those thermodynamic destiny guys, you don’t have to do much to further your vision of the good. As water flows downhill, the universe will realize it for you, because you simply defined it to be the natural outcome of the dog-eat-dog churn. But if you want a world where the weak are enduringly safe and free and equal, you have to constantly be pumping water to places that would naturally be high and dry. Men are stronger and more aggressive than women, adults are much smarter and stronger than children, humans are overwhelmingly more powerful than animals. Enduring safety and freedom and equality for women and children and animals requires a greater force stemming the natural tide.

The grand leftist project seems like it basically requires building a Leviathan.4 And in a more mundane near-term sense, it requires winning elections. Or running activist organizations that manage to avoid eating themselves from the inside endlessly “problematizing” their own leadership.5 To change the rules you have to first win the game. And it feels like the very act of winning makes you less left-wing. It seems like you have to absorb some of the best virtues of the right: cutting out deadweight, doing what it takes, playing for real money. As you shape yourself into the kind of creature that wins, you might cultivate a bit of disgust for your own weakness, or weakness writ large.

As a leftist in my heart, I share the left's foibles. Building and wielding power has always felt boring, stressful, and crass. This made working for a multi-billion-dollar foundation a bit of an odd fit. In fall 2024, after eight years at Open Phil, I burned out and took four months off. A big reason for this was struggling to have a positive and healthy relationship to the fact that Open Phil was a place where so much power had pooled. It was like the government of AI safety. Everyone wants something from you, everyone's watching you, everyone has opinions and no one's happy. It's a position that breeds tightness and conservatism. I came to find it tough to talk to my community and move through the world the way I wanted to.

I decided I wanted to be powerless and free. I drafted a whole dramatic coming-out post about how I was quitting and I was going to let my freak flag fly and I was entering a whole new era where I wasn’t even really trying to maximize impact anymore, only Truth.

Around then I got a drink with one of my oldest friends, a product manager at Apple. He said I sounded like the engineers he knew at Apple who just couldn’t handle the corporate politics of getting Apple to do things differently. Maybe they tried to make good things happen for a while, but eventually burned out and quit. And his attitude toward them was basically: “Sure, you can leave if you need to. But it’s not noble that you couldn’t handle the work of gaining and wielding power. It doesn’t make you a better person.”

I didn’t end up leaving Open Phil in 2024. I got a new opportunity to be helpful and influential there, and I took it because Open Phil is a really powerful institution working toward important goals I share, and it’s important to shape it and accelerate it. I did leave a year later, to join an organization that’s a much better fit for my natural drive to just understand the truth and explain it as best I can. I may never be as ruthless and disciplined about maximizing impact as my colleagues who most thrive at Open Phil. But I am staying in the game, because it matters to win.

1

I have this sense from a general memory of high school European history, but also here’s ChatGPT and Claude on some of the relevant history, though note that my prompt to them was leading: “Right now the left is stereotypically against markets and capitalism. But I feel like there was a time in the past, when monarchs and feudalism were dominant, when markets were more left-wing. Am I off-base? Can you analyze the validity of this hypothesis with specific citations to historical moments?” I was too lazy to come up with a more neutral prompt or do any other investigation for the purpose of this blog post.

2

One of my favorite posts on old LessWrong is Why are individual IQ differences ok? It captured something about my moral worldview I had not seen crystallized anywhere else.

3

One way this could be achieved is if kids had extremely advanced AI advisors that were deeply aligned to supporting the decisions this child will eventually make as it grows, with none of the pride and ego and preconceived notions that human parents bring to the matter. This may sound impossible (How is it well-defined “what the kid will eventually decide”, and what do you do about all the decisions you're forced to make in the meantime?), but I think it's an only slightly more extreme version of the problem of aligning superintelligent AI advisors to support adults — we are as infants compared to our distant future selves. (This idea might also sound creepy and deeply wrong-headed, and it might be.)

4

Which, yes, is in itself extremely scary. Meditating on that, especially in the context of superintelligent AI, has made me less left-wing. It might be better to tolerate a huge amount of inequality and distributed brutality doled out by many chieftains locked in a state of anarchic competition than to pool enough power into a single authority that it can actually stem the tides of competition. But not all Leviathans are created equal, and I remain optimistic about designing a trustworthy Leviathan. I think the existence of liberal democratic states that combine vast capacity for violence with internal immune systems that help limit its use, is a reason for hope. That…would have been more comfortable to say twenty or thirty years ago, but I think the point still stands. We haven't explored the structure of governments very much as a species, and I think we can build on the best of liberalism, and superhuman AI could bring technology to both negotiate and enforce much more elaborate and subtle contracts much more effectively.

5

This SNL sketch about the phenomenon is one of my favorites, and has a right-wing ethos. It throws in some liberal shibboleths (e.g. a comment about the annoying employees being rich white kids), but fundamentally it’s making fun of the pathetic weak new recruits whose hysterics and insubordination threaten to weaken the greater organism of the ship at a time when it has to hold fast against an external threat.

item.title: Tempering hardcoreness
item.content:encoded:
There’s a kind of young guy who itches to accept great pain and risk for some glorious quest. Depending on other features of his brain and his particular place and time and upbringing, this could manifest as enlisting to fight the Nazis in World War II, free soloing El Capitan, trying to conquer the Achaemenid empire, grinding on the next great B2B SaaS unicorn, training all day to become a UFC fighter or a concert pianist, trying to build a machine god to conquer death, etc.

One popular way to channel this drive is to become super hardcore about a totalizing ideology or cause. You could become a Franciscan monk or join ISIS or try to achieve nirvana. And of course, you could become a hardcore EA (I highly recommend!).

I myself am not that hardcore. I do try to maintain a paranoid vigilance about the big picture of my career (am I really doing the highest impact thing I could be doing?), but I’ve put most of the hardcoreness points I’ve got into that. I spend a lot more money on myself than I need to for productivity or sustainability. I’m not vegan, nor am I doing an optimized IQ-maxxing diet featuring a bunch of oily fish or whatever. I don’t streamline my morning routine or optimize my keyboard layout or cycle through various stimulant cocktails to work 13 hour days. I devote generous amounts of time and money and energy to the soft and frivolous things in life like throwing parties and getting manis and participating in weddings and snuggling babies. I aspire to have children of my own, though this will be another massive expenditure of time and money that pulls away from helping the world.

I’m surrounded by twenty-something dudes who work 80 hour weeks to save the world, commuting the five minute walk from their Spartan group apartment to our shared office at 5:30 am every day, taking short breaks for spirited shop talk over vegan lunches and dinners in the building. They make generous salaries saving the world (unlike in the old days of EA) but then turn around and donate most of it.

Like seven years ago my main reaction to these guys would have been to feel terrible about my own sloth and decadence, but at this point I’ve gotten over myself / grown old and given up (career EAs age in dog years). There is a measure of guilt — and when I catch the right mood I still try to see if I can scrounge up another hardcoreness point or two — but at this point a greater measure of acceptance about my own drive. I’m left mainly with enormous affection, gratitude, and admiration for them all. I’m impatient for the day they make me obsolete.1

But as grateful as I am for these guys, I’m also grateful that the actual real-life community they find themselves in subtly de-radicalizes them. In this context, they are generally extremely productive and delightful people who I think are having a huge positive impact on the world. But it is unfortunately very easy for me to imagine many of these same people instead getting swept up in something like FTX, and having a giant negative impact and a miserable time.2

Don’t get me wrong, the scene is still a scaffold that takes intense young people as input and elicits like 3000 hours of high-energy x-risk reducing work out of them per year for a while. It’s not exactly for the faint of heart, and it’s not like “de-radicalization” is the point exactly. But relative to so many other ways this community could easily have been, it has that effect.

Firstly, the established senior folks in the scene, who have an outsized impact on the culture and discourse, are truly, deeply not naive utilitarians — but at the same time they’re also not the kind of disingenuously sanctimonious scolds who hand down simplistic rules that the young and hungry and hardcore would be tempted to roll their eyes at. A lot of the people who’ve been around for a few years are like the next Pokemon evolution of the slightly-crazed 22 year old Benthamite. They have a lot of empathy for that headspace, they have thought deeply about the gnarly questions that come up when you push that worldview to its brink, they can engage in lengthy and subtle debates about those topics.

And people are fundamentally tolerant of one another’s personal choices, and resist engaging in purity death-spirals (partly thanks to the cultural example of the aforementioned established folks). Within every ideological scene, the internal logic and social incentives tend to push you toward embodying a more extreme version of that ideology, whether that’s competing to declare more and more banal views “problematic” in some social justice circles or competing to say the most shocking and transgressive things you can in some young right circles. In the AI x-risk scene, this force certainly exists, but is empirically weaker than in most analogous communities. I find the social pressure is often channeled toward things like whether you have good arguments for your career choice rather than whether you’re working too little or spending too much.

This means that if you ever run out of steam being a monastic vegan who works 80 hours a week, you can pretty seamlessly transition into a reducetarian dad who works 40 hours a week. You don’t have to lose your friends or professional community, you’ll probably still have more impact year on year as your experience grows, you’ll look back with pride on how much you accomplished in a more intense season of your life — and you won’t end up like, in jail for the greatest financial crime in history or anything like that.

1

I’m thinking about 3.5 weeks before the AIs do.

2

Individuals vary, but on average, I don’t think these young utilitarians have the kind of discriminating eye that would have warned them away from Alameda and FTX in its heady early days.

item.title: Being a woman
item.content:encoded:
I’m surrounded by men who seem mostly cis by default, who don’t seem to really think about their masculinity much (and maybe just don’t think much about their interiority, period?). Meanwhile, I’ve always had Big Feelings about being a woman. Aella’s how to be respected as a teen girl is perhaps the single most relatable article I’ve ever read on the internet.

As a little girl I was an instinctive, fiery feminist. I grew up watching old Indian movies from the 50s and 60s. A disturbing number of them have the following basic plot: “Long-suffering wife remains slavishly obedient to degenerate abusive husband, eventually reforming him with the power of her devotion, whereupon she falls to his feet in joy.” I remember being six or seven, shaking with hot rage at the society that would make movies like those. I would ask my dad how this could possibly be acceptable. He’s a staunch believer in individual rights, and he would validate my outrage at what amounted to sex-based slavery. But he was also a heterodox intellectual type who’d probably have been a rat if that were a thing in the 70s, and my anger would often inspire him to share his frank musings on how men came to rule the world. One day, he was like “You know, Ayn Rand1 once said that if women ran the world, we would still be living in grass huts.”2

When I started lurking on LessWrong as a high school freshman, I fixated on the discourse going on there about evolutionary psychology and sex differences in IQ and personality and capacity for greatness and of course all the attendant pickup artistry. Looking back now, I don’t think this stuff was all that big a part of the conversation happening there at the time? But that was the discourse that hurt the most, and therefore that was the discourse I had to pay attention to. The worst sin I could imagine committing was to disengage from discourse because it implied that my kind was inferior. Because if it hurt it was probably right, right? And if it was right, then I had a moral obligation to obsessively form the most accurate possible understanding of the exact nature and degree of my inferiority.

I interpret a lot of things about myself through the lens of my sex. Many dudes come into EA because they’re into moneyball and then realize they can moneyball the good — but I was a little girl who liked to take care of babies, and I realized there were way too many babies who needed me, and I had to get smart about it if I wanted to save them all.

I often feel a deep frustration that I don’t have the ambition and chutzpah it takes to really do the biggest things, where the really real impact lies. That thing where some guys can get arbitrarily intense about arbitrary goals, from speedrunning Minecraft to crypto investing? What the fuck is that? My brain does not do that. I can just feel it, that nagging sensation that I didn’t evolve to take wild swings to get the girl, I evolved to be anxious and choosy, to find protection and hide underneath it and minimize negative surprises. I feel like I am so easily cowed, so easily tired. When I’m depressed I sometimes wish I could be killed and replaced with someone better optimized for impact, and I feel like that someone would be a man.3

Of course, the creature truly optimized for impact would have no gender, no recognizably human personality at all. As long as we all must remain our deeply sub-optimal selves, there is a niche in the world for my kind of brain.

I built my career in a male-dominated pocket of an already male-dominated field. AI risk is probably 75% male, and “insane speculation about the future of AI” is north of 90%. Several times a week I find myself in a conference room or lunch table or slack discussion where it’s me and ten to fifteen dudes, and often what I bring is a woman’s touch. I’m the Oracle at Delphi channeling a half dozen raving Apollos, distilling wacky ideas so people can understand them, doing the empathetic work of modeling an audience and distilling ideas so people can engage with them. I’m grateful that there’s this act of care which comes so naturally to me can come in handy for the world.

1

My dad’s a hardcore Objectivist.

2

ChatGPT says this is an apocryphal quote. EDIT: Lam in the comments points out that it’s from Camille Paglia in Sexual Personae.

3

I have a few specific men in mind, though also to be fair at least one woman.

item.title: Exit rights
item.description: What should we have to endure?
item.content:encoded:
In eighth grade we had to do a persuasive speech in English class, and I talked about how voluntary euthanasia should clearly be legal. One of my favorite authors, Terry Pratchett, had just been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s and embarked on what would become a long battle for the right to die on his own terms — one he would ultimately lose when he died from complications of dementia eight years later.

I’ve always thought it’s monstrous to criminalize suicide in any form. It feels perverse to take someone who already felt life was too much to bear and force them to keep going (at taxpayer’s expense) in what’s often an even more miserable existence in a prison or hospital bed. While we don’t actually prosecute people for attempting suicide anymore,1 we do try to make it pretty hard to kill yourself. If you disclose serious suicidal ideation to a teacher or counselor or other authority figure, they’re usually under legal obligations or intense social pressure to immediately report you to institutions that will aggressively try to thwart you.

This attitude doesn’t sit right with me. Yes, it’s tragic to make a rash mistake and cut off what could have been a long happy life, but it’s also horrifying to be trapped in misery. We should try to do so much better for people than nothing — but in case we fail, we should be very wary of stripping them of a choice in the matter. You can do worse than nothing. The right to opt out of a bad situation feels like the foundation on which all other rights are built, and the right to opt out of life itself feels like the bottommost brick of that foundation.

The next brick is the right to physically move away. Perhaps the most despicable thing about evil regimes like North Korea and Iran is that they don’t let people freely leave.2 If there was just one piece of international law I could magically enforce, it would be exit rights. This wouldn’t right all the wrongs overnight, but it would instantly give a huge number of people a real shot at a better life, and create an incentive gradient that would improve conditions even for those who stay.

The ability to freely cut off ties with people is another type of exit right. No-fault divorce, established in most of the Western world by the mid-twentieth century, is probably the most important of these.3 This one is more complicated, because (in the good parts of the world) marriage is a contract you enter into freely. The libertarian in me wants to allow people to make whatever contracts they want, and the game theorist in me understands that sometimes cutting off your options increases your utility. The social conservative in me sees the appeal of something like a covenant marriage. But while covenant marriage contracts as they exist seem fine enough,4 I don’t think marriages that fully cut off the possibility of divorce should be allowed. I don’t think people should be allowed to sell themselves into slavery, even though this is in some sense violating their right to freely enter into a contract. The person you’ll become in the future is in many ways a separate being from you right now, and I don’t think you should have an unbounded license to override that person’s exit rights.5

Even when they nominally have exit rights, many people in bad situations today don’t have the practical or psychological means to leave, or better places that would be willing to take them in, or even a real understanding of what better places are out there. I hope we can do much better in the future. In a future where most people live as digital minds, we could create an ever-present “exit button” that lets you instantly retreat to a secure and pleasant personal sanctuary that you control entirely and can stay in as long as you want. It should be just as easy as hitting the circle button on a video game controller — pause, exit to menu. Intuitively, I’d want to make it exceedingly difficult for anyone (including yourself) to remove the button.

This means that if we’re living in a simulation right now, it violates the strong exit rights I intuitively want for simulated people. In a good scenario, maybe an outside version of myself consented to be put in a video game about the early Singularity and to have her memory of the choice wiped — but even so, I, right now, don’t have the right to exit to something better than death.6 Maybe that’s okay? Even if people shouldn’t be allowed to permanently forsake exit rights for their future selves, not every person-moment has to be wholly free to break from person-moments in the recent past. For all I know, maybe I’m woken up every year and offered the choice to leave the video game, and I always chose to stay. I think that would be okay.

1

I was wrong about the state of the law around this. Growing up I had the sense that suicide was illegal, and this was one of many injustices in the world that fueled my teenage outrage. But according to ChatGPT suicide had actually been decriminalized in the US in the mid-twentieth century. This didn’t fully happen in India until 2017 though, which might be why I thought this (if I got my understanding from my parents).

2

Iran is better than North Korea on this front. Men have free-ish ability to leave, and exit restrictions fall disproportionately on women, who need permission from male guardians to get a passport.

3

Another one that’s dear to my heart is the right of children to leave their parents. My parents were perfectly nice, but I had a strong interest in legal emancipation as a teenager and got pretty deep into researching the laws in California. It was out of some combination of taking pride in independence, and making a political statement for a cause I believed in — kind of like a feminist who refuses to marry even if she’s in a loving and positive relationship with a man, to protest the patriarchal institution of marriage. Emancipation of minors is definitely more practically thorny than allowing divorce, but I believe it should be much more widespread and normalized for older kids. With future technology, we could try to construct meaningful exit rights even for very young children.

4

In fact, actual covenant marriages (a stricter, legally distinct variant of marriage recognized in a few red states) seem kinda weaksauce compared to the most hardcore thing I would tolerate, since one of the paths to divorce seems to be just living apart for one or two years? Needless to say, while this is a thing pushed by “trad” social conservatives, it is a far more humane and egalitarian institution than marriage was for the vast majority of human history.

5

You might reasonably object that committing suicide is violating the right of your future, potentially happier, self to exist. I don’t have a perfect answer to this, but I do think the distinction between “negative rights” and “positive rights” matters to me here. I am not entirely a utilitarian, not even in my personal morality and certainly not in my political philosophy. You are obligated not to hurt others far more strongly than you are obligated to help them, including doing them the often profound service of allowing them to exist. To me, refraining from suicide when your life is not currently worth living feels like a supererogatory altruism toward your future self — whereas signing your future self up to be enslaved or tortured feels like a violation of their rights.
